activities.anchor: laid end to end like train carriages
activities.caption: command to contraction — rebuild the ratchet
activities.name: mesSarcomereOrder

config.prompt: From nervous command to a shortened muscle — order the sliding-filament steps:
items: The nervous system commands a contraction — calcium is released
Binding sites on the actin are exposed
Myosin heads ratchet the filaments past each other — they slide, they do not shorten
The Z-discs at each sarcomere's ends are pulled together
Millions of sarcomeres sum — the whole muscle shortens
config.why: Muscles only pull — they cannot push — so every joint is served by antagonistic pairs: biceps flex the elbow while triceps extend it.

activities.anchor: Bones are levers, joints are fulcrums
activities.caption: file the body's levers by class
activities.name: mesLeverSort

config.prompt: The body contains all three lever classes — file each example:

items.label: nodding the head — the neck muscles' effort sits between the skull's load and the joint
the rarest class in the body
rising onto tiptoes — effort arm longer than load arm, mechanical advantage
the biceps curl — muscle inserts a few centimetres from the joint
holding a 10 kg weight steady — the muscle pulls with roughly 70–90 kg
the body's default: speed and range bought at the cost of force

config.why: Force in muscle is proportional to physiological cross-sectional area — which is why strength training builds girth, and why the pennate arrangements of calf and quad pack more fibres into the same limb volume.

activities.anchor: The striking fact is how little
activities.caption: size the body's cash reserve
activities.name: mesAtpEst

config.prompt: Only about 80–100 g of ATP sits in the body at any instant. Roughly how many seconds of maximal effort does that store fund?
config.why: A couple of seconds — performance is a recharging problem, not a storage one, and the three energy systems are three ways of regenerating ATP from ADP.
config.context: Rigor mortis is the recharging stopped: without ATP bound, the myosin heads cannot detach.

activities.caption: mark where the phosphocreatine tank runs dry
activities.name: mesPcrPlace

config.prompt: All-out work has begun. Place the moment the phosphocreatine reserve empties:
config.why: PCr fuels roughly 6–10 seconds of all-out work, then needs 3–5 minutes of rest to refill — which is why sprint training runs short repeats with long recoveries and a powerlifter waits minutes between attempts.

activities.anchor: The old story said lactic acid builds up
activities.caption: which lactate curve is the trained athlete's?
activities.name: mesLactateTrace

config.prompt: Blood lactate against workload — which curve belongs to the trained athlete?

curves.label: threshold arrives early in the effort
threshold sits at a higher fraction of maximum

config.why: Endurance training improves exactly this recycling — the trained athlete burns lactate as fast as they make it, and the lactate threshold is among the best predictors of distance-running performance, better than raw VO₂max alone.

activities.anchor: The rate is limited by oxygen delivery
activities.caption: the crossover concept — pair each fuel with its trading profile
activities.name: mesFuelMatch

config.prompt: The aerobic system's fuels trade off — match each to its profile:

pairs.right: plentiful — tens of thousands of kcal even in lean athletes — but slower to access, needing oxygen
fast, and required once the effort outpaces oxygen supply
roughly 1,600–2,000 kcal — the bottleneck that empties near 30 km
roughly 30–34 ATP per glucose, versus 2 from anaerobic glycolysis

config.why: 'Hitting the wall' in a marathon is a glycogen-depletion event — which is why fuelling matters as much as the training.

activities.anchor: you must stay in the low-intensity
activities.caption: the fat-burning zone vs the harder run — drag the divider
activities.name: mesZoneCompare

config.prompt: Two sessions side by side — drag the divider:

before.label: the low-intensity walk
before.text: a larger share of the energy comes from fat — but fewer total calories burned per minute

after.label: the harder run
after.text: a smaller share from fat, more from carbohydrate — yet more fat grams and more total energy per minute

config.why: Fat loss tracks total energy expended, and a harder session spends more calories from every fuel — the walk and the run both burn fat; the run simply burns more per minute.

activities.anchor: The classic exam trap is treating the systems as time zones
activities.caption: one line of this pricing is wrong — click it
activities.name: mesMixSpot

config.prompt: One line of this event-pricing is wrong — click it:
lines: The 400 m is roughly 55–60% aerobic — a majority comes from oxygen-dependent pathways.
PCr depletion caps the sprint; acidosis caps the 60–90 second effort; glycogen, heat and central drive cap the long ones.
config.correction: The 1500 m is about 80–85% aerobic — endurance events flip the mix, which is why their training looks nothing like sprint training.
config.why: Each number shifts the prescription: the 400 m runner needs the glycolytic engine and a serious aerobic base to speed lactate clearance between repeats.
